title: CLIN-SUMM: Incremental Longitudinal Summarization of Clinical Notes Enables Scalable Representation and Early Disease Prediction
authors: D'Souza, V.; Pace, D. F.; Azhir, A.; Nargesi, A.; Holbrook, E. B.; He, W.; Naumann, T.; Friedman, S.; Atlas, S. J.; Anderson, C. D.; Hung, J.; Maddah, M.
abstract: Electronic health records contain years of longitudinal clinical notes rich in evolving patient information, yet their volume, redundancy, and fragmentation limit clinical usability and scalable modeling. We present CLIN-SUMM (Clinical Longitudinal Insight from Notes using Summarization), a framework that restructures summarization as a longitudinal representation problem. Rather than collapsing histories into static summaries, CLIN-SUMM incrementally constructs structured, categorized, date-partitioned patient representations, summarizing only newly documented information at each encounter while preserving temporal fidelity without access to future data. This standardized representation can be computed once and reused across downstream tasks, thereby decoupling narrative processing from prediction. Across 12,356 Massachusetts General Hospital patients, CLIN-SUMM achieved 75% word reduction while maintaining high clinician-rated correctness and completeness. Using dementia as a case study, fine-tuning Clinical ModernBERT on CLIN-SUMM summaries yielded AUROC 0.84 for diagnosis and outperformed raw notes for 3-year risk prediction (AUROC 0.66 vs. 0.63). Combining summary-based predictions with structured EHR variables improved 3-year prediction to AUROC 0.69, reaching 0.74 among patients younger than 75 years, with longitudinal analyses demonstrating progressive risk separation years before a formal diagnosis. CLIN-SUMM summaries also enabled efficient extraction of longitudinal medication trajectories, complementing structured EHR data by recovering medication information documented in notes, with high dose agreement for matched records. CLIN-SUMM provides a scalable representation layer for clinical review and longitudinal machine learning, enhancing disease modeling, risk prediction, and other longitudinal reasoning tasks.

infographic.key_insight: CLIN-SUMM reduced clinical-note word count by 75% while creating reusable longitudinal summaries that improved dementia risk prediction over raw notes.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Structured, time-aware summaries could make lengthy patient histories easier to review and support longitudinal research and prediction.
method: Incrementally summarize newly documented information at each encounter without accessing future data.
Organize patient information into structured categories and date partitions.
Fine-tune Clinical ModernBERT on summaries and combine predictions with structured EHR variables.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 12,356 Massachusetts General Hospital patients, summaries had high clinician-rated correctness and completeness; 3-year dementia prediction AUROC was 0.66 versus 0.63 with raw notes, rising to 0.69 with structured EHR variables.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports a single-institution evaluation; generalizability and prospective clinical utility remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: CLIN-SUMM: Incremental Longitudinal Summarization of Clinical Notes Enables Scalable Representation and Early Disease Prediction

title: Comprehensive real-world utilization, treatment trajectories, and outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors across cancer types: the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort
authors: Ha, L. T.; Ver Donck, F.; Bassez, I.; Oeste, C. L.; Vulsteke, C.; Delombaerde, D.; Hens, D.; Prenen, H.; Croes, L.; De Meulenaere, A.; Debruyne, P. R.; Verhaert, M.; Aspeslagh, S.; Brusselaers, N.; Verbiest, A.
abstract: BackgroundImmune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer treatment, yet evidence on their utilization, treatment trajectories, and effectiveness in routine clinical practice remains limited. We characterized real-world ICI use and outcomes across cancer types using the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort and explored differences between real-world and pivotal trial outcomes. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults receiving ICIs across four Belgian hospitals. Structured and unstructured electronic health record data were harmonized using the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) and natural language processing. We evaluated overall survival (OS), time on treatment (ToT), time to next treatment (TTNT), ICI discontinuation (>12-week treatment gap without re-initiation), and post-discontinuation survival. OS was descriptively compared with pivotal trials, and prognostic factors were assessed using multivariable Cox regression. An interactive public dashboard was developed to enable exploration of cohort characteristics, treatment patterns, and outcomes. ResultsAmong 3,231 ICI-treated patients, 2,514 (77.8%) had metastatic disease. Among metastatic patients, 568 (22.6%) discontinued ICI without subsequent systemic therapy. Median post-discontinuation OS was 21.4 months (95% CI 16.5-37.2), with 49.1% alive at 24 months. ToT and TTNT were generally shorter than OS, particularly in melanoma (median OS 78 months; ToT 7 months; TTNT 26 months). Real-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal trials. ECOG [≥]2 was associated with poorer OS than ECOG 0-1 (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82-2.60). In NSCLC patients receiving pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, survival with ECOG 0-1 more closely approximated trial outcomes, whereas survival with ECOG [≥]2 was substantially poorer. ConclusionsReal-world ICI treatment trajectories extend beyond active treatment, with some patients experiencing prolonged survival after discontinuation. Differences between real-world and trial outcomes highlight the importance of patient characteristics, particularly performance status, when interpreting trial evidence in routine care. FAIR-ICI provides a scalable framework for evaluating real-world immunotherapy effectiveness, treatment trajectories, and future investigations of treatment-related toxicity. HighlightsO_LIFAIR-ICI studied 3,231 patients across four Belgian hospitals and provides an interactive dashboard for subgroup exploration. C_LIO_LIAmong metastatic patients, 22.6% stopped ICIs without subsequent systemic therapy, with 49.1% alive at 24 months after stopping. C_LIO_LITime on treatment and time to next treatment were generally shorter than overall survival. C_LIO_LIReal-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal clinical trials. C_LIO_LIPoor ECOG performance status was strongly associated with shorter survival and may contribute to trial-real-world differences. C_LI

infographic.key_insight: Real-world immune checkpoint inhibitor outcomes varied across cancers, with some patients surviving well beyond treatment discontinuation and poorer performance status associated with shorter survival.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Treatment duration alone may not capture long-term outcomes, and patient performance status is important when interpreting pivotal trial results in routine care.
method: Retrospective cohort of 3,231 adults receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors across four Belgian hospitals.
Structured and unstructured electronic health records harmonized using OMOP-CDM and natural language processing.
Survival and treatment trajectories assessed, with descriptive trial comparisons and multivariable Cox regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 568 metastatic patients who discontinued immunotherapy without subsequent systemic therapy, median post-discontinuation survival was 21.4 months; ECOG ≥2 was associated with poorer overall survival than ECOG 0–1 (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82–2.60).
infographic.watch_item: Observational, descriptive comparisons cannot establish causal differences from trials or show that discontinuing treatment improves survival.
infographic.paper_title: Comprehensive real-world utilization, treatment trajectories, and outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors across cancer types: the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort

title: AI-Based MRI Radiomics for Preoperative Detection of Tumor Deposits in Rectal Cancer: A Bivariate Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-analysis
authors: Alsaied, M. A.; Hegazy, M.; Saleh, M. M.; Barakat, B.; Ibrahim, O. R.; Abdelrazek, H. M.; Nazemi, S.; El-Hussuna, A.; Shalaby, M.
abstract: Background: In rectal cancer (RC), tumor deposits (TDs) are clinically important as they are associated with a negative impact on prognosis and affect risk stratification as well as management plans. MRI radiomics combined with artificial intelligence (AI) has been explored for non-invasive preoperative TDs detection. However, results vary across studies; therefore, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool their diagnostic test accuracy (DTA). Methods: This systematic review and DTA meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy and reported in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA). Databases were screened for DTA studies of MRI-based radiomics predicting TDs in adult RC patients with histopathology as reference. Results: Nine studies (2589 patients) were identified. Across included studies, the bivariate meta-analysis showed pooled sensitivity of 0.765 (95% CI 0.714 - 0.809) and specificity of 0.790 (95% CI 0.750 - 0.825), with overall AUC of 0.845 and very low heterogeneity (I2 = 7.3%). In validation datasets, diagnostic performance remained consistent (AUC 0.806), with pooled sensitivity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809) and specificity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809). For MRI modality, T2 weighted image (T2WI) showed higher sensitivity (0.745) than T2WI plus diffusion weighted image (DWI) (0.697), while T2WI+DWI had higher specificity (0.809 vs 0.737) and AUC (0.829 vs 0.796), with no significant subgroup differences (p[≥]0.192). Models combining radiomics with clinical/radiological variables achieved significantly higher sensitivity (0.842 vs 0.657, p<0.001) and higher AUC (0.827 vs 0.752), with comparable specificity. Conclusion: MRI-based radiomics demonstrates good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in RC. The integration of radiomics with clinical or imaging features increases the accuracy of identification. Amongst the MRI modalities, models that utilize the combination of T2WI plus DWI are more accurate than those using T2WI or DWI only.

infographic.key_insight: AI-based MRI radiomics showed good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in rectal cancer, with pooled sensitivity of 76.5%, specificity of 79.0%, and AUC of 0.845.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Non-invasive identification of tumor deposits could support preoperative risk stratification because these deposits are associated with worse prognosis.
method: Systematic review and bivariate diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis of 9 studies involving 2,589 patients.
Evaluated MRI radiomics against histopathology as the reference standard.
Compared MRI sequences and radiomics-only models with models incorporating clinical or radiological variables.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation datasets showed an AUC of 0.806; combined radiomics–clinical/radiological models had higher sensitivity than radiomics-only models (84.2% vs 65.7%; p<0.001).
infographic.watch_item: MRI sequence subgroup differences were not statistically significant, so superiority of T2WI plus DWI is not established.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Based MRI Radiomics for Preoperative Detection of Tumor Deposits in Rectal Cancer: A Bivariate Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-analysis

title: Micro-fragmented adipose tissue reprogrammes the systemic molecular landscape of inflammatory knee osteoarthritis
authors: Primorac, D.; Molnar, V.; Brlek, P.; Bulic, L.; Jelec, Z.; Prosenc Zmrzljak, U.; Klaric, T.; Lauc, G.; Malod-Dognin, N.; Przulj, N.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis affects an estimated 374 million people and has no approved disease-modifying treatment. In our double-blind randomised trial (ISRCTN88966184), intra-articular micro-fragmented adipose tissue (MFAT) outperformed hyaluronic acid (HA) on pain, function and cartilage composition -- but clinical endpoints alone cannot say whether the disease changed or only the symptoms. Here we answer that question from the blood. Using an interpretable AI data-fusion framework based on non-negative matrix tri-factorisation, we integrated longitudinal plasma proteomics, N-glycomics and miRNA transcriptomics with patient genetics and prior molecular networks at baseline, one and six months, resolving 93 gene and 30 miRNA pathways, almost all significantly enriched in Gene Ontology Biological Process and Reactome annotations. By six months the two injections had left sharply distinct molecular fingerprints. HA remained dominated by canonical OA pathogenesis, including the cartilage-degrading effectors MMP13 and LIMK2 and persistent markers of synovial inflammation. MFAT instead shifted the systemic landscape towards chondroprotection, anti-inflammatory signalling and bone-cartilage homeostasis, prioritising effectors including SIRT7 and NDUFC1. These are, to our knowledge, the first in vivo human data to explain why a regenerative therapy outperforms viscosupplementation in knee osteoarthritis, and they place MFAT on the disease-modifying rather than the symptomatic side of that divide.

infographic.key_insight: AI-integrated blood profiling linked MFAT treatment to molecular patterns consistent with cartilage protection and reduced inflammation, distinct from those following hyaluronic acid.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings suggest potential disease-modifying effects in knee osteoarthritis, but blood molecular signatures alone do not establish disease modification.
method: Analysed samples from a double-blind randomised trial comparing MFAT with hyaluronic acid.
Integrated plasma proteomics, N-glycomics, miRNA profiles, genetics and molecular networks using interpretable non-negative matrix tri-factorisation.
Tracked molecular patterns at baseline, one month and six months.
infographic.evidence_signal: The analysis resolved 93 gene and 30 miRNA pathways, with distinct six-month treatment signatures accompanying reported MFAT advantages in pain, function and cartilage composition.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract omits sample size and effect sizes; independent validation and longer-term structural outcomes are needed to substantiate disease modification.
infographic.paper_title: Micro-fragmented adipose tissue reprogrammes the systemic molecular landscape of inflammatory knee osteoarthritis

title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort
authors: Nowroozi, A.; Bondarenko, M.; Brar, S. S.; Haas, B.; Brown, J.; Rustagi, A.; Graham, B.; Hudson, M.; Su, G.; Yala, A.; Sohn, J. H.
abstract: Objective: We aimed to 1) evaluate whether AI algorithms could identify a very low-risk sub-population Lung-RADS 1/2 cases suitable for a safe switch to biennial screening, and 2) externally validate Sybil, an imaging-based deep learning lung cancer risk prediction tool. Materials and methods: We gathered all lung cancer screenings (LCSs) from a tertiary safety-net hospital (n=3120, up to September 2024), manually extracted relevant clinical data, and analyzed Sybil's performance across various subgroups, with a specific focus on Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases. We simulated LCS interval extension using Sybil and the Brock model risk scores calibrated on a subset of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). Confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. Results: The median follow-up was 2.3 years (interquartile range 1.5-3.1), with a total 6-year cancer incidence rate of 2.3% (72/3120). Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases comprised 90.5% of our scans. Sybil's overall area under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.819 to 0.912; while its 2-year AUC for Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases was 0.746. In the screening interval extension simulation, calibrating for a 30% shift to biennial screening translated into 33.8% of negative screens in our data being safely extended using Sybil, with no delayed cancers. The Brock model demonstrated an AUC of 0.513 on our data, with a sensitivity of 18.2% using the 1.5% threshold. Conclusion: Sybil has the potential to safely extend LCS intervals for low-risk individuals, reducing radiology workload and opening spots for life-saving new screenings.

infographic.key_insight: In a retrospective simulation, Sybil identified 33.8% of negative lung cancer screens for biennial screening with no delayed cancers observed.
infographic.clinical_relevance: AI-guided screening intervals could reduce radiology workload and expand screening capacity, pending prospective validation.
method: Retrospectively analyzed 3,120 lung cancer screenings from a tertiary safety-net hospital.
Externally evaluated Sybil, focusing on Lung-RADS 1–2 cases.
Simulated interval extension using Sybil and Brock risk scores calibrated on an NLST subset.
infographic.evidence_signal: Sybil achieved overall AUCs of 0.819–0.912 and a 2-year AUC of 0.746 in Lung-RADS 1–2 cases; 72 cancers occurred among 3,120 screenings.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center retrospective simulations with median follow-up of 2.3 years do not establish the safety of longer screening intervals in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort

title: AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free enrichment reveal tumor heterogeneity, genomic relatedness, and divergence in malignant effusions
authors: Magbanua, M. J. M.; Huppert, L. A.; Cruz, J.; Goudreau, J.; Zhou, S.; Yin, K.; Stejskal, P.; Gill, t.; Carelli, R.; Kim, J.; Hsie, L.; Wang, M.; Lian, Z.; Manepalli, S.; Phelan, M.; Ray, M.; Johnson, C.; Nieto, J.; Schneider, E. C.; Mavropoulos, A.; Delson, A. L.; Simmons, C.; Parizadeh, A.; Crawford, J.; Bruck, M.; Her, L.; Barnett, V.; Cabrera, A. M.; Melisko, M.; Balassanian, R.; Rugo, H. S.; van 't Veer, L.; Jovic, A.; Devine, W. P.; Sayaman, R. W.; Salek, M.; Masaeli, M.; Rosenbluth, J.; Goodarzi, H.
abstract: BackgroundMalignant effusions are clinically accessible yet underutilized sources of metastatic tumor cells. However, abundant background immune cells complicate tumor cell isolation and molecular characterization. We integrate AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free tumor cell enrichment with genomic profiling to characterize phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. MethodsWe applied a pre-trained deep learning model to brightfield images of single cells from malignant effusions of 10 patients with metastatic breast cancer to extract morphological features, quantify tumor cell fraction (TCF), and guide label-free microfluidic enrichment. We profiled copy-number alterations and somatic mutations in enriched tumor cell fractions and compared them with available matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors. ResultsAI-powered single-cell morphological analysis identified putative tumor cells in all 10 patients (median TCF, 5.4%; range, 0.51-15.8%; n = 25 samples). AI estimates of major immune-cell populations varied across patients and samples and correlated with flow cytometry measurements (n = 21 paired samples, Pearson r = 0.69-0.75). Unsupervised analysis identified four tumor cell morphotypes, revealing intra- and inter-patient morphological heterogeneity and longitudinal variation in morphotype composition. Genomic profiling of enriched tumor cell fractions by low-pass whole-genome sequencing (n = 26 samples) and whole-exome sequencing (n = 24 samples) identified copy-number alterations and somatic mutations, with tumor fraction influencing genomic signal strength. Comparisons of genomic profiles from tumor cell-enriched fractions with matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors revealed shared genomic alterations, providing orthogonal support for tumor origin and relatedness, while differences across analytes revealed genomic divergence and tumor heterogeneity. ConclusionAI-powered analysis leverages single-cell morphology for tumor cell identification and label-free enrichment, while integration with genomic profiling enables simultaneous interrogation of phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. This approach expands the potential of malignant effusions for liquid biopsy applications and biomarker development and discovery.

infographic.key_insight: AI-guided single-cell imaging and label-free enrichment revealed morphological heterogeneity and shared and divergent genomic alterations in metastatic breast cancer effusions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Malignant effusions may offer an accessible source for studying metastatic tumor diversity, although clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Applied a pretrained deep-learning model to single-cell brightfield images to estimate tumor fractions and characterize morphology.
Used morphology-guided microfluidics to enrich tumor cells without labels.
Profiled enriched-cell genomes and compared them with available matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 10 patients, imaging identified putative tumor cells in 25 samples (median tumor fraction, 5.4%); immune-cell estimates correlated with flow cytometry (r = 0.69–0.75), and genomic profiling supported tumor origin and relatedness.
infographic.watch_item: The small cohort and tumor-fraction-dependent genomic signal warrant broader validation before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free enrichment reveal tumor heterogeneity, genomic relatedness, and divergence in malignant effusions

title: Current gaps in downstream applications of fMRI foundation models: lessons learned from BrainLM & BrainHarmonix on Prevent-AD
authors: Wang, H.-T.; Pichet Binette, A.; Sainath, P.; Farrugia, N.; Villeneuve, S.; Bellec, L.
abstract: Foundation models have driven major advancements in the language and vision domains, as seen in the popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, and a growing number of studies are bringing the approach to human brain imaging. Whether these models are ready for independent researchers to use on clinical datasets has yet to be examined. We evaluated two recent fMRI foundation models, BrainLM and BrainHarmonix, on PreventAD, a dataset on adults with a family history of Alzheimers disease. We compared features from frozen and fine-tuned models against two baselines: functional connectivity and a dummy classifier that always predicts the most common class. The sample includes 343 subjects who passed quality control, with a subset of 218 who had amyloid PET imaging. We tested four prediction targets: sex, age, progression to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and {beta}-amyloid burden. Both models required substantial changes to the released code. BrainLMs own data preparation workflow did not produce stable fine-tuning, which we achieved only after switching to a standard workflow implemented with the library Nilearn. BrainHarmonixs documentation did not specify how to normalize new data, so we resolved this by testing different alternatives. For sex, functional connectivity outperformed all foundation model features. For age group, the best foundation model feature, taken from BrainHarmonixs structural (T1-weighted) encoder, slightly exceeded functional connectivity, but the difference was not significant. For MCI and {beta}-amyloid, no feature exceeded the dummy classifier in accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) stayed near chance for all features. For both clinical targets, the most precise feature came from fine-tuned BrainLM, meaning a larger share of its positive predictions were correct than for functional connectivity, but neither difference reached statistical significance. These results suggested that the strong transfer to new tasks seen in large language models cannot yet be assumed for fMRI foundation models, and that both models required code adaptation that would preclude their streamlined adoption by independent groups. We recommend that future studies provide standardized data workflows and always report functional connectivity and dummy classifier baselines. For clinical targets with strong class imbalance, studies should report several metrics, including precision.

infographic.key_insight: BrainLM and BrainHarmonix did not demonstrate a clear predictive advantage over simple baselines on PreventAD, highlighting gaps in fMRI foundation-model transfer.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings do not establish reliable prediction of mild cognitive impairment progression or β-amyloid burden in adults with a family history of Alzheimer’s disease.
method: Evaluated frozen and fine-tuned foundation-model features against functional connectivity and a majority-class dummy classifier.
Tested sex, age group, progression to mild cognitive impairment, and β-amyloid burden.
Adapted released code, preprocessing, and normalization to enable evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study included 343 quality-controlled participants, 218 with amyloid PET; neither clinical target exceeded dummy-classifier accuracy, and AUC remained near chance.
infographic.watch_item: Substantial code changes and unclear preprocessing requirements limited streamlined independent use of both models.
infographic.paper_title: Current gaps in downstream applications of fMRI foundation models: lessons learned from BrainLM & BrainHarmonix on Prevent-AD

title: Enhancing deep sleep with auditory stimulation to boost cognitive training responsiveness in people with Parkinson's disease and mild cognitive impairment: Rationale and design of the double-blind randomized controlled trial PD-CogT-Sleep
authors: Ophey, A.; Kleinsorge, M. T.; Wallimann, N. A.; Maric, A.; Loosli, S. V.; Mollenhauer, B.; Balint, B.; Huber, R.; Baumann, C. R.; Kalbe, E.; Schreiner, S. J.
abstract: BackgroundCognitive training (CogT) is an established non-pharmacological intervention for people with Parkinsons disease (PD) and mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI). However, overall effects on cognitive outcomes are small to moderate and interindividually highly heterogeneous. Sleep -especially deep sleep-could be an important determinant of CogT responsiveness in PD, and may have beneficial effects on PD pathophysiology. Therefore, the enhancement of deep sleep by phase-targeted auditory stimulation (PTAS) could strengthen the effects of CogT on cognitive symptoms and counteract disease progression. MethodsPD-CogT-Sleep is a monocentric, partly decentralized, double-blind, randomized sham-controlled trial that combines two remotely delivered non-pharmacological interventions, to assess the additive effect of PTAS on digital CogT responsiveness in people with PD-MCI. The primary outcome is executive functions; Secondary and exploratory outcomes include further cognitive functions, participant-reported outcome measures, blood-based biomarkers, and high-density sleep electroencephalography markers. Outcomes are assessed at baseline, five weeks post-allocation and at 3-month follow-up. We aim to consecutively recruit N=50 participants, who will be randomized 1:1 to receive CogT+PTAS or CogT+Sham. DiscussionThe PD-CogT-Sleep study integrates wearable and digital technologies to systematically combine a novel, non-invasive, sleep-enhancing intervention (PTAS) with established CogT to improve cognition and evaluate PTAS disease-modifying potential through its effects on blood-based biomarkers in PD-MCI. The expected results will foster our understanding of the interplay of sleep, cognition, and neurodegeneration, and may guide further development of safe, feasible, scalable, patient-centered, technology-based non-pharmacological interventions counteracting cognitive decline in neurodegenerative diseases. infographic.clinical_relevance: If effective, this remotely delivered, non-pharmacological approach could help improve cognitive training responsiveness, but benefits are not yet established.

Participants randomized 1:1 to digital cognitive training plus phase-targeted auditory stimulation or sham stimulation.

title: A Reproducible Decomposed Large Language Model Pipeline for Structured Abstraction of Multimodal Neuroimaging Reports: Development and Independent Validation in 1,669 Emergency Department Encounters for Dizziness and Vertigo
authors: Shahani, J.; Ousta, A. R.; Shaulov, S.; El-Sherif, Y.
abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and independently validate a decomposed, modality-specific large language model (LLM) pipeline that abstracts structured variables from the free-text neuroimaging reports of a multimodal stroke workup, and to validate the resulting structured dataset for reuse in downstream research. Materials and MethodsA frozen pipeline (temperature 0) extracting 22 variables across CT head, CT angiography, CT perfusion, and MRI brain was applied to 1,669 ED encounters for dizziness or vertigo; 11 variables were pre-specified as primary (Tier 1). Reproducibility used three same-session runs and a nine-week re-run; three frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.5 Flash) measured cross-model agreement (Cohens/Fleiss {kappa}). Accuracy was assessed in an independent 200-encounter cohort (150 random, 50 enriched for rare findings); 100 were double-read by two blinded reviewers with discordances adjudicated. ResultsTest-retest reproducibility was high (Tier 1 Fleiss {kappa}=0.993; 99.8% exact) and stable nine weeks later ({kappa}=0.992); inter-model agreement was {kappa}=0.962. Against the adjudicated reference, pooled Tier 1 accuracy was 0.971 to 0.988 across models (Cohens {kappa} 0.959 to 0.982), comparable to inter-reviewer agreement ({kappa}=0.932). Accuracy was 0.980 to 0.983 in random and 0.955 to 0.977 in enriched encounters (agreement on model-flagged findings, not sensitivity). DiscussionA decomposed LLM pipeline produced reproducible, model-portable, stable, and accurate multimodal abstraction. Because schema design and validation are up-front costs, such pipelines scale to larger research cohorts. ConclusionThe quantified per-field error rates support reuse of this dataset with field-specific review, and such pipelines offer a practical path to large-scale, reproducible research datasets.

infographic.key_insight: A decomposed, modality-specific LLM pipeline extracted structured neuroimaging data with high reproducibility and accuracy across three models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The pipeline could support reusable research datasets from emergency dizziness and vertigo imaging reports, with field-specific review rather than autonomous clinical decision-making.
method: Extracted 22 variables across CT head, CT angiography, CT perfusion, and brain MRI; 11 were primary outcomes.
Applied a frozen, temperature-0 pipeline to 1,669 emergency department encounters.
Tested repeatability, nine-week stability, cross-model agreement, and accuracy against an adjudicated reference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Independent validation in 200 encounters found pooled primary-variable accuracy of 97.1–98.8%; test–retest exact agreement was 99.8%.
infographic.watch_item: Results for rare-finding-enriched encounters measure agreement on model-flagged findings, not sensitivity; field-specific error review remains important.
infographic.paper_title: A Reproducible Decomposed Large Language Model Pipeline for Structured Abstraction of Multimodal Neuroimaging Reports: Development and Independent Validation in 1,669 Emergency Department Encounters for Dizziness and Vertigo

title: A Knowledge Database of Physical Activity Interventions for Hypertension using Large Language Models
authors: Li, C.; Obioha, C.; Cui, X.; Zhou, X.; Rosenzweig, A.; Wang, M.
abstract: Physical exercise lowers blood pressure, but guidelines provide broad recommendations that rarely account for age, comorbidities, medications and hypertension severity. A structured, queryable resource of exercise interventions for hypertension is lacking, while manual curation is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We present PAHD (Physical Activity for Hypertension Database), built with large language models (LLMs). An LLM screened 2,548 PubMed records through title-and-abstract and full-text assessment, selecting 255 studies. LLMs extracted arms, exercise protocols, participant characteristics, and outcomes, with two LLMs cross-checking study structure and each value linked to a verbatim quote. Programmatic integration generated 17,273 standardized records from 253 studies, one per reported comparison. Against adjudicated benchmarks, screening achieved 86.3% recall and 80.6% precision, and extraction 90.1% recall and 90.5% precision for blood pressure values. A clinician-facing portal retrieves studies matched to patients hypertension stage and comorbidities. PAHD is a reusable, traceable evidence resource for personalized exercise interventions in hypertension.

infographic.key_insight: PAHD uses large language models to turn hypertension exercise studies into a structured, queryable evidence database with source-linked values.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A clinician-facing portal retrieves studies matched to hypertension stage and comorbidities, supporting evidence review rather than establishing individualized exercise prescriptions.
method: An LLM screened 2,548 PubMed records and selected 255 studies.
LLMs extracted study arms, exercise protocols, participant characteristics and outcomes, with dual-LLM structure checks and verbatim source quotes.
Programmatic integration produced 17,273 standardized comparison records from 253 studies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against adjudicated benchmarks, screening achieved 86.3% recall and 80.6% precision; blood pressure value extraction achieved 90.1% recall and 90.5% precision.
infographic.watch_item: Screening and extraction errors remain, and the abstract does not report validation of patient-level recommendations or clinical outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: A Knowledge Database of Physical Activity Interventions for Hypertension using Large Language Models

title: Combined Use of Topic-Analysis and LLMs on Online Peer-to-Peer Medicaid Discussions to Detect the Impact of HR1 on Individuals Medicaid Experience Across The US
abstract: Medicaid is a government program providing benefits to 1 in 5 people in the US, including medical care for children and adults, long-term care for the elderly, and home/community-based services for the disabled[1]. Effective January 1st 2027, HR1 (One Big Beautiful Bill) passed by Congress will implement new administrative requirements to Medicaid expected to strip benefits from 1.8 million adults, children, and seniors[2]. As each US state administers Medicaid independently, the timing, frequency, and severity of those losses may vary across states. Monitoring that human impact requires an detailed ongoing view of affected individuals and their families. To monitor the human-impact of HR1, this work develops a proof-of-concept using topic analysis and LLMs to generate detailed categorization of individuals' Medicaid experiences across multiple states and over time.

infographic.key_insight: This proof-of-concept combines topic analysis and large language models to categorize Medicaid experiences shared online and support monitoring of HR1’s human impact.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Tracking reported coverage and administrative challenges could help identify barriers to care, but the abstract does not establish clinical benefits.
method: Analyze online peer-to-peer Medicaid discussions.
Combine topic analysis with LLM-based categorization.
Organize reported experiences across states and over time.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a proof-of-concept but reports no dataset size, evaluation metrics, or validation results.
infographic.watch_item: Online discussions may not represent all Medicaid beneficiaries, and attributing reported experiences to HR1 requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Combined Use of Topic-Analysis and LLMs on Online Peer-to-Peer Medicaid Discussions to Detect the Impact of HR1 on Individuals Medicaid Experience Across The US

title: Clinical Prediction Model Performance Metrics Cluster at Arbitrary Thresholds and are Incorrectly Reported in High-Ranking Journals: An Observational Meta-Research Study
authors: Gibson, A. D.; Borg, D. N.; White, N. M.; Barnett, A.
abstract: Background Previous research has shown that clinical prediction models have likely been 'hacked' to meet arbitrary performance thresholds. However, this work only assessed abstracts, could not identify models with a perfect AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) of 1, and did not examine other performance metrics. Methods We collected data from full texts and validated a large language model to extract data from a random sample of Q1 journal articles for 2025. We examined if hacking occurred in the AUC value, sensitivity and specificity, and checked if articles correctly reported the AUC value from corresponding receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Results We identified 2,001 prediction model articles that reported 15,656 AUC values. We found a striking excess of results near perfect prediction and at multiples of five and ten for the AUC, sensitivity and specificity, indicating likely manipulated data, methods or publication bias. Around 1 in 40 AUC values were reported outside of their confidence intervals, and around 1 in 8 ROC curves did not match their reported AUC value. Conclusion We have shown that not only the AUC value, but the sensitivity and specificity are being hacked, likely to help the authors publish their paper at the cost of evidence for practice. Excess models that are not representative of their true performance may misguide clinicians, distort the literature, and make it harder to find prediction models that are useful for practice.

infographic.key_insight: Clinical prediction model metrics clustered near perfection and at multiples of five and ten, suggesting selective reporting, methodological manipulation, or publication bias.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Inflated or incorrectly reported performance could mislead clinicians about prediction models’ usefulness in practice.
method: Examined full texts from a random sample of 2025 Q1 journal articles.
Validated a large language model for data extraction.
Assessed metric clustering and checked reported AUCs against confidence intervals and ROC curves.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 2,001 articles reporting 15,656 AUC values, around 1 in 40 AUCs fell outside their confidence intervals and around 1 in 8 ROC curves did not match the reported AUC.
infographic.watch_item: This observational analysis identifies suspicious patterns and reporting inconsistencies but cannot establish intentional manipulation.
infographic.paper_title: Clinical Prediction Model Performance Metrics Cluster at Arbitrary Thresholds and are Incorrectly Reported in High-Ranking Journals: An Observational Meta-Research Study

title: Capturing additional variance in impact of adolescent depression from free text: proof of concept and preliminary results
authors: Matar, A. Y.; Lossio-Ventura, J. A.; Pereira, F.; Nielson, D. M.
abstract: Depression in adolescents has grown in prevalence in the past decade. Despite indications of differences in symptom presentation, measurement properties, and treatment response between adolescents and adults, research is dominated by adult participants. Qualitative work has identified symptomatic and functional domains important to depressed adolescents and those around them; however, there remains little quantitative evidence of how these domains relate to the functional impact of the disorder. In this preregistered study, we use adolescent self-report (n = 153) and parent-report (n = 106) responses in the depression section of the Development and Well-Being Assessment (DAWBA) to examine what information relevant to reported depression impact may be missing from its structured symptom-scale. We apply Large Language Models (LLMs) to participant free-text answers to extract information on a taxonomy of 80 outcomes. Through a sequential residual stacking framework that estimates incremental information in symptom sum-scores (S ), item-level symptom-scale answers (Q), and LLM-derived text representations (T ), we find that parent text contains information relevant to their report of depression impact that is not available in the structured symptom-scale, with the largest contributions concentrated in functioning-related domains (e.g., professional responsibilities, social exclusion, autonomy, coping). No such evidence was found in adolescent self-reports. Given the moderate sample size, these results are preliminary. Nonetheless, we provide a proof-of-concept framework for extracting information from open-ended free text in large existing datasets, and estimating incremental information across sources, which could be applied to uncover specific aspects of adolescent mental disorders across populations.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-derived features from parent free text captured additional information about reported adolescent depression impact beyond structured symptoms, while adolescent self-reports showed no such evidence.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Parent narratives may complement structured assessments by capturing functioning-related concerns such as social exclusion, autonomy, coping, and responsibilities.
method: Analyzed adolescent and parent responses to the DAWBA depression section.
Used LLMs to extract information across a taxonomy of 80 outcomes from free text.
Applied sequential residual stacking to estimate incremental information from symptom totals, individual items, and text features.
infographic.evidence_signal: The preregistered study included 153 adolescent self-reports and 106 parent reports, with additional text-based information found only in parent reports.
infographic.watch_item: The moderate sample size makes these findings preliminary and does not establish clinical utility.
infographic.paper_title: Capturing additional variance in impact of adolescent depression from free text: proof of concept and preliminary results

title: Automated Segmentation of Intracranial Arteries on 4D Flow MRI for Hemodynamic Quantification
authors: Zhang, J.; Verschuur, A. S.; van Ooij, P.; Schrauben, E. M.; Bakker, M. K.; Nam, K. M.; van der Schaaf, I. C.; Tax, C. M. W.
abstract: Accurate vessel segmentation is essential for reliable hemodynamic quantification in 4D Flow MRI. Automated segmentation with deep learning offers a promising alternative to the time-consuming, operator-dependent manual segmentation, but its application is often hindered by the scarcity of labeled datasets. Moreover, while a previous study has evaluated the impact of automated vs manual segmentation on downstream intracranial hemodynamic quantification, it remains to be explored whether variability between different automated segmentation methods affects hemodynamic quantification significantly, particularly in the context of intracranial 7T 4D Flow MRI. We investigated a transfer learning-based intracranial artery segmentation model using a 3D full-resolution nnU-Net, pretrained on 355 TOF-MRA scans and fine-tuned on 11 7T 4D Flow MRI scans. The model was compared with two published models: a direct-transfer U-Net pretrained only on TOF-MRA without 4D Flow MRI fine-tuning, and a DenseNet U-Net trained from scratch on the same 11 7T 4D Flow MRI scans. Segmentation performance was evaluated against the manual reference on test sets with different resolutions and the impact on downstream hemodynamic quantification was assessed. The transfer learning-based nnU-Net achieved the highest Dice score (>0.85), the lowest HD95 ([~]3 mm), and the highest ICCs in cross-sectional area (0.62-0.87, except PCAs) and mean blood flow (0.78- 0.98). For wall shear stress (WSS) quantification, the transfer learning-based nnU-Net segmentations achieved the closest agreement with the manual reference (mean = 1.57 {+/-} 0.63 Pa, ICC = 0.96; max = 2.16 {+/-} 1.05 Pa, ICC = 0.97) and minimal bias ([≤] 1.7%), whereas U-Net and DenseNet U-Net showed systematic under-(-5%) and overestimation (+7%), respectively. However, several vessel segments, including the ACA for DenseNet U-Net and the BA for U-Net, showed statistically significant differences (ANOVA post-hoc correction P < 0.05) in the flow-related metrics when compared with the manual reference. These results suggest that a transfer learning-based nnU-Net can provide accurate automated intracranial artery segmentation for 7T 4D Flow MRI. Differences among automated segmentation pipelines and associated analysis regions were linked to differences in downstream hemodynamic estimates.

infographic.key_insight: A transfer learning–based nnU-Net achieved the strongest intracranial artery segmentation and closest agreement with manual-reference hemodynamic measurements among three models tested.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated segmentation could reduce manual workload for 7T 4D Flow MRI research, but model choice can affect measured blood flow and wall shear stress.
method: Pretrained a 3D full-resolution nnU-Net on 355 TOF-MRA scans and fine-tuned it on 11 7T 4D Flow MRI scans.
Compared it with a direct-transfer U-Net and a DenseNet U-Net trained from scratch.
Evaluated segmentation and downstream hemodynamic measurements against manual references across test sets with different resolutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The nnU-Net achieved Dice >0.85, HD95 approximately 3 mm, and wall shear stress ICCs of 0.96–0.97 with bias ≤1.7%.
infographic.watch_item: Only 11 7T scans were used for fine-tuning, and agreement varied by vessel, warranting broader validation before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Segmentation of Intracranial Arteries on 4D Flow MRI for Hemodynamic Quantification

title: Using Vision and Large Language Models for Psychological Intervention Competency Assessment: A Pilot Study of Agreement with Clinician Ratings
authors: Liu, Y.; Leever, W.; Stanco, M.; Shook, Z.; Addico, P.; Gleeson, S.; Nugroho, F.; Varney, G.; Youngstrom, E.; Sezgin, E.
abstract: Introduction: Supervision in psychological intervention training is limited by the time needed to evaluate simulated sessions. We tested a Vision Language Model (VLM) and Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline that assesses competency from verbal and nonverbal communication. Method: Gemini-3.1-Pro was used to annotate behaviors in 25 simulated therapy videos and incorporate them into transcripts, and ChatGPT-6.1-Sol rated them against the ENACT scale. Two clinicians verified VLM-identified behaviors and four independently rated each video. Agreement was estimated with Gwet's AC1 and ICC. Results: Of 1,558 VLM-identified behaviors, 70% were confirmed by both clinicians and 93% by at least one. AI-clinician agreement on therapeutic behavior attributes (AC1=0.73, 95% CI 0.70-0.76) approached between-clinician agreement (0.75, 0.72-0.78). AI-clinician ICCs on therapeutic domain levels (median 0.57) were modestly lower than between-clinician ICCs (0.67). Discussion: The pipeline agreed with clinicians nearly as well as clinicians agreed with each other and shows promise as a supplementary evaluator in therapist training.

infographic.key_insight: In a pilot study of 25 simulated therapy videos, AI ratings approached clinician agreement on therapeutic behavior attributes but showed lower agreement on domain-level competency.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The pipeline may supplement competency assessment in therapist training, rather than replace clinician supervision.
method: A vision-language model annotated verbal and nonverbal behaviors and incorporated them into transcripts.
A large language model rated competency using the ENACT scale.
Two clinicians verified detected behaviors; four independently rated each video.
infographic.evidence_signal: Clinicians jointly confirmed 70% of 1,558 AI-detected behaviors; AI–clinician attribute agreement was AC1=0.73 versus 0.75 between clinicians, while median domain-level ICCs were 0.57 versus 0.67.
infographic.watch_item: The small, simulated-session sample limits generalizability; validation in real-world training settings is needed.
infographic.paper_title: Using Vision and Large Language Models for Psychological Intervention Competency Assessment: A Pilot Study of Agreement with Clinician Ratings
